name: The Stroke Economy
oneLine: Steiner's claim that five childhood rules - don't give, don't ask, don't accept, don't reject, don't self-stroke - manufacture an artificial scarcity out of something that was never actually limited.
whatYouDid: You played a resident of Fuzzbrook breaking each of the five rules in turn - complimenting a stranger, asking directly whether your work landed, accepting praise without deflecting it - and felt the town's quiet pushback every single time.
confusion: People treat stroke scarcity as just how things are; the tell is that Steiner traces it to five specific, learned rules - which means it was taught, which means it can be unlearned.

fromBook.quote: Don't give strokes if you have them to give.

expand.definition: Steiner's five stroke-economy rules: don't give strokes if you have them to give, don't ask for strokes when you need them, don't accept strokes if you want them, don't reject strokes when you don't want them, don't give yourself strokes.
expand.otherFraming: TA Today describes the same mechanism from the parent's side: a situation in which strokes could be available in a limitless supply is transformed into a situation in which the supply is low and the price parents can extract for them is high.
expand.tryThisToday: Pick just one rule and break it once today - give an unprompted compliment, or say thank you without deflecting it.
